content.text: There is a particular silence that follows a wreck, and it is not the silence of peace. The sea keeps no calendar, which is either its great honesty or its great indifference. An old friend visiting after years away brings the past with them, uninvited but not unwelcome.

My predecessor left a note pinned inside the lamp room door: mind the wind, it changes its mind before you do. The bread was better that winter, though no one could say exactly why. A long apprenticeship teaches humility faster than it teaches skill, and in the correct order.

On clear nights the beam swept the water like a hand searching a dark room for a dropped key. The train timetable was more aspiration than fact, and everyone along the line understood as much. A candle burns down evenly only if you trim the wick, a lesson repeated in every household.

I have come to think of the tower less as a building than as a very patient argument against the dark. The orchard gave less fruit that year but of a better, denser sweetness. A stranger's kindness on a hard day is remembered longer than most kindnesses from family.

The gulls nested in the rock below and complained, as they always did, about everything at once. The wind off the water carried salt far enough inland to whiten the window glass by spring. A journal kept honestly becomes, without meaning to, a kind of second memory.

A letter came twice a month by the supply boat, and twice a month I read it standing at the rail. The market emptied by four, leaving only the smell of what had been sold there. An old dog knows the sound of the right footsteps long before anyone else in the house does.

Storms here do not announce themselves; they simply arrive, the way grief arrives, mid-sentence. The harvest moon that year hung low enough to seem, briefly, close. A debt repaid on time is remembered less than one repaid a day late.

I learned to mend the winding gear myself, because the mainland was three hours away on a good sea. The workshop smelled of sawdust and, faintly, of the coffee no one ever finished. A letter that arrives too late still says something true, even if the moment has passed.

The keeper before the keeper before me carved his initials into the stair rail, and I have never sanded them out. The garden wall held the day's heat long after the sun itself had gone down. An empty house is loud in a way a full one never manages to be.

When the light held through a bad night I felt something close to pride, though pride is a poor word for it. The apprentice years pass slowly at the time and quickly in the remembering. A well-worn tool fits the hand better than any new one, however well made.

The horizon at dusk turned the colour of a bruise healing, violet giving way to a tired green. The evening train was always half empty, and always exactly on time. An old photograph tells you what a person looked like and almost nothing about who they were.

I counted the ships that passed safely as another man might count blessings, which is to say I counted them at all. The bakery opened before the rest of the street had decided the day had begun. A long correspondence, kept up faithfully, is its own kind of small monument.

There is a ledger for the oil, a ledger for the weather, and no ledger at all for what the solitude costs. The frost came early that year and stripped the orchard almost overnight. An honest account of a hard season reads, afterward, like a much easier one than it was.

By April the ice had gone from the rocks and the birds came back as though nothing had happened. The workshop door stuck in wet weather, a fault no one ever quite got around to fixing. A river town keeps different hours than a market town, and neither much minds the other's.

The lamp turned once every eight seconds, and I had long since stopped counting the beats between. The last light of the day fell across the table in a way that made finishing supper feel unhurried. An old coat, kept for sentiment, still fits better than most people expect.

Fog came up the channel that morning the way smoke fills a room no one thinks to leave. The harbor quieted by evening to the sound of ropes against the pilings and little else. A neighbor's lamp, lit before dawn, was as good as a clock to anyone passing.

From the gallery the sea looked less like water than like a great grey animal breathing in its sleep. The season turned the way seasons do, without asking anyone's permission first. An unfinished letter is, in its way, more honest than a finished one.

I kept the log in a hand steadier than my nerves, because the log would outlast both of us. The workshop ledger recorded debts in pencil and settlements in ink, and rarely confused the two. A well-worn path through a wood is a kind of quiet agreement among everyone who uses it.

A ship passed close enough that I heard her bell before I saw her, which is its own kind of warning. The morning fog burned off by nine most days, later on the days it mattered least. An old friend's handwriting is recognisable at a glance, long after the face has grown less familiar.

The oil ran low twice that winter, and twice I walked the six miles to the store rather than let the light fail. The market square filled slowly and emptied all at once, as though on a signal no one gave aloud. A garden gate left open is, more often than not, simply an invitation no one has withdrawn.

The lamp oil was rationed that winter, and the evenings grew, by necessity, quieter for it. An old ledger, found later, tells a fuller story than the person who kept it ever meant to leave behind. The wind changed direction twice in a single afternoon, which the fishermen took as its own kind of warning.

A long winter makes the first warm day feel larger than the weather alone accounts for. The workshop's apprentices came and went, but the smell of the place never really changed. An orchard in bloom is briefly, almost embarrassingly, more beautiful than it has any right to be.

The evening post brought less news than expected and somehow felt heavier for it. A house passed down through a family keeps, in its floors and doorframes, a record no deed can match. The harbor at first light belonged to the gulls and the earliest of the fishing boats.

An old debt of kindness is rarely called in outright, only quietly remembered. The bread rose slowly in the cold kitchen, and the whole house smelled the better for waiting. A traveller's stories improve with each telling, a fact both teller and listener quietly agree to overlook.

The workshop closed for the season the way it always did, mid-sentence, with a job left half finished. An old road, no longer maintained, is still walkable long after it stops being useful. The frost patterns on the window that January were, by common agreement, the finest anyone could recall.

A letter home, written honestly, is harder to write than any other kind. The village kept its own time, twenty minutes behind the railway, and saw no reason to change. An empty ledger page is, in its way, as informative as a full one.
